newsitem.title: USA: Cotton jumps on exports, gas prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Cotton jumps on exports, gas prices fall.

text.p: Cotton prices rose Thursday on news of an unexpected jump in exports this past week, while silver prices fell to an 18-month low amid an apparent move by powerful commodity funds to drive prices lower.
Gasoline prices ended sharply lower as talk of imports from Europe arriving on top of ample U.S. stocks fuelled concerns of oversupply.

The cotton market focused on an Agriculture Department report Thursday the United States exported 151,600 bales of cotton during the week ended Sept. 12. This was double the previous week's volume and 2-1/2 times greater than the four-week average.

Cotton analysts said low prices two weeks ago attracted foreign buyers, mainly from Asia. The Agriculture Department said China bought 73,500 bales, Indonesia 23,200, Hong Kong 21,900 and Japan 20,500.
"Every time we get into the lower 70's (cents per pound), we can sell cotton," said Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider & Co. Inc.
During the five days prior to Sept. 12, cotton traded near 72.50 cents per pound, she said.

Prices were also supported by forecasts for rain this weekend in Texas and along the southern Mississippi River. Rain on the mature cotton can damage the lint, lessening the supply of high quality cotton.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, the October contract closed 0.80 cent higher at 74.25 cents per pound.
Silver prices tumbled largely because wealthy technical traders sold based on chart trends rather than supply and demand news.

"There was no change in the fundamentals, just some fund selling and (sell) stop executions which fed on themselves when silver failed to quickly bounce back from the break of $5.00," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
"Prospects for another large shortfall between world supply and demand should prevent silver prices from dropping much below the $5.00 level," Rinehimer said.

At New York's Commodity Exchange, December silver ended down 15.8 cents at $4.940 an ounce, after sinking to an 18 month low of $4.925. In the bullion market, spot silver also hit an 18-month-low of $4.90 an ounce.
Soft red winter wheat futures at the Chicago Board of Trade closed lower as persistent reminders of stiff competition from overseas customers weighed on the market.
U.S. wheat is costlier than foreign supplies, plus Europe announced it will subsidise wheat to boost export sales.

"With the rebate (subsidy) in Europe this morning it just showed you the trend of the market is down. They're giving it away again," said Steve Bruce, a grain trader with E.D. and F. Man International.
Grain traders said early Thursday in Paris the European Union (EU) granted licenses to export 237,470 metric tons of soft wheat with the EU subsidising the sales.
CBOT December wheat closed 4 cents to 10-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with December down 7-1/2 cents at $4.16-3/4.
Gasoline for October delivery settled down 1.74 cent at 61.32 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) after falling as low as 60.40 cents during the day.
"It's a combination of imports when we have ample supply, and the gasoline season being now over," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil.
Gasoline demand traditionally peaks during the summer, and inventory draws during the summer were considered lackluster by traders.
Meanwhile, shipping sources have noticed a sharp increase in charters for gasoline shipments from Europe to the United States in September.
October crude oil settled off 35 cents to $23.54 a barrel and October heating oil settled 1.10 cent lower to 66.77 cents a gallon on profit-taking.

Crude and heating oil rallied strongly Wednesday after inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute showed a much smaller-than-expected build in heating oil. Heating oil stocks are at historical lows as winter approaches.
